claim: Oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system exhibit significant variability in the number of myelin sheaths that are supported by each cell, ranging from 1 to 50.
source: Oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system exhibit significant variability in the number of myelin sheaths that are supported by each cell, ranging from 1 to 50 (1-8).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (1-8) referencing prior literature.

claim: Myelin production during development is dynamic and involves both sheath formation and loss.
source: Myelin production during development is dynamic and involves both sheath formation and loss (3, 9-13).
evidence: Supported by citations (3, 9-13) referencing prior literature.

claim: Oligodendrocytes repetitively ensheathed the same axons multiple times before any stable sheaths were formed.
source: Surprisingly, we found that oligodendrocytes repetitively ensheathed the same axons multiple times before any stable sheaths were formed.
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Repetitive ensheathment was independent of neuronal activity.
source: Importantly, this repetitive ensheathment was independent of neuronal activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing tricaine and pancuronium bromide anesthesia.

claim: ~80–90% of ensheathments initiated by oligodendrocytes always disappeared.
source: However, ~80–90% of these ensheathments always disappeared, an unexpectedly high, but consistent rate of loss.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of time-lapse imaging data.

claim: The dynamics of the ensheathment process indicated rapid membrane turnover as ensheathments were formed and lost repetitively on each axon.
source: The dynamics of this process indicated rapid membrane turnover as ensheathments were formed and lost repetitively on each axon.
evidence: Based on inference from observed repetitive ensheathment dynamics.

claim: Oligodendrocytes over-expressing a dominant-negative mutant form of Rab5 did not show a change in early sheath initiation dynamics but did lose a higher percentage of ensheathments in the later stabilization phase.
source: Oligodendrocytes over-expressing this mutant did not show a change in early sheath initiation dynamics but did lose a higher percentage of ensheathments in the later stabilization phase.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Rab5 dominant-negative mutant expression.

claim: Oligodendrocyte sheath number is heterogeneous because each cell repetitively initiates a variable number of total ensheathments that are resolved through a consistent stabilization rate.
source: Overall, oligodendrocyte sheath number is heterogeneous because each cell repetitively initiates a variable number of total ensheathments that are resolved through a consistent stabilization rate.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data on ensheathment dynamics.

claim: There are ~2-fold more myelinating oligodendrocytes in the ventral tracts compared to the dorsal tracts.
source: There are ~2-fold more myelinating oligodendrocytes in the ventral tracts compared to the dorsal tracts (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by cell count data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Oligodendrocytes in the dorsal region of the spinal cord had more sheaths on average than oligodendrocytes in the ventral region.
source: Importantly, oligodendrocytes in the dorsal region of the spinal cord had more sheaths on average than oligodendrocytes in the ventral region (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: No statistically significant differences in average sheath length or the total sheath length were found when comparing dorsal and ventral oligodendrocytes.
source: No statistically significant differences in average sheath length or the total sheath length were found when comparing these groups (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: Each oligodendrocyte repetitively ensheathed the same axonal domain an average of 2–3 times before any stable sheaths were formed.
source: Unexpectedly, each oligodendrocyte repetitively ensheathed the same axonal domain an average of 2–3 times before any stable sheaths were formed (Figure 2D, E [T0', T15', T45', T60']).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Of the 25 axonal domains analyzed, 14 of them ended up with a stabilized sheath and 11 were lost.
source: Of the 25 axonal domains analyzed, 14 of them ended up with a stabilized sheath (Figure 2F) and 11 were lost (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figures 2F and 2G.

claim: 72% of axonal domains were ensheathed more than once.
source: The total number of ensheathment attempts on each axonal domain ranged from 1 to 6, and 72% of these domains were ensheathed more than once.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of axonal ensheathment data.

claim: Tricaine is a sodium channel blocker that silences action potentials throughout the CNS.
source: This drug is a sodium channel blocker that silences action potentials throughout the CNS.
evidence: Based on established pharmacological knowledge about tricaine.

claim: Neuronal activity is important for myelination.
source: Neuronal activity is important for myelination, and it is possible that the repetitive axonal ensheathment that we observed could result from silencing neuronal activity.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge and prior literature.

claim: Pancuronium bromide is a neuromuscular blocking drug that does not dampen neuronal activity in the CNS.
source: We anesthetized each larva in either tricaine or pancuronium bromide, which is a neuromuscular blocking drug that does not dampen neuronal activity in the CNS (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK538346/).
evidence: Supported by citation to external reference.

claim: Pancuronium bromide has been used previously in zebrafish activity-dependent myelination studies.
source: It has also been used previously in zebrafish activity-dependent myelination studies (Hughes and Appel, 2020; Koudelka et al., 2016; Hughes and Appel, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: There was essentially no difference in the average number of times an oligodendrocyte ensheathed the same axonal domain when comparing tricaine and pancuronium bromide anesthesia.
source: Importantly, there was essentially no difference in the average number of times an oligodendrocyte ensheathed the same axonal domain when comparing these forms of anesthesia (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3B-D.

claim: 43% of the axonal domains were stabilized at the end of the imaging paradigm for the tricaine group and 55% were stabilized for the pancuronium bromide group.
source: We also found that 43% of the domains were stabilized (16 of 37) at the end of the imaging paradigm for the tricaine group and 55% were stabilized (16 of 29) for the pancuronium bromide group (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: A Fisher's exact test found no significant difference between the stabilization rates of tricaine and pancuronium bromide groups.
source: A Fisher's exact test found no significant difference between these values.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: There was a measurable difference in the CNS activity of larvae anesthetized in tricaine vs pancuronium bromide.
source: As a follow-up to this work, we performed a quality control experiment to demonstrate that there was a measurable difference in the CNS activity of larvae anesthetized in tricaine vs pancuronium bromide in our experiment.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging experiment data.

claim: There was no significant difference in the number of calcium transients in the pre- and post-videos for the controls, but there was a clear reduction in transients after the tricaine spike.
source: There was no significant difference in the number of calcium transients in the pre- and post-videos for the controls, but there was a clear reduction in transients after the tricaine spike (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: There was a clear difference in the percentage of calcium transients in the tricaine spiked group relative to the controls.
source: There was still a clear difference in the percentage of calcium transients in the tricaine spiked group relative to the controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by normalized calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The repetitive ensheathment phenomenon is independent of neuronal activity.
source: Collectively, this experiment allows us to more strongly conclude that the repetitive ensheathment phenomenon that we observed in Figures 2 and 3 is independent of neuronal activity.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data comparing tricaine and pancuronium bromide.

claim: For the tricaine condition, 72.6% of all axonal domains were ensheathed more than once.
source: Further assessment of the two axonal ensheathment experiments from Figures 2 and 3 indicates that for the tricaine condition, 72.6% of all axonal domains were ensheathed more than once (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: 65.5% of axonal domains were ensheathed more than once for the pancuronium bromide group.
source: Similarly, 65.5% of domains were ensheathed more than once for the pancuronium bromide group.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of the pancuronium bromide data.

claim: In 100% of instances, each axonal domain was repetitively ensheathed by the same oligodendrocyte.
source: In 100% of these instances, each axonal domain was repetitively ensheathed by the same oligodendrocyte (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The same cell process performs each ensheathment and seems to maintain continuous contact with the axon ~63–68% of the time.
source: Additionally, the same cell process performs each ensheathment and seems to maintain continuous contact with the axon ~63–68% of the time (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D, see Materials and methods for more details).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: Maintaining contact with the axon could be important for sheath formation.
source: This suggests that maintaining contact with the axon could be important for sheath formation.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observation that processes maintaining contact have higher stabilization rates.

claim: There was no significant difference in the average number of repetitive ensheathments for an axonal domain based on whether a sheath becomes stabilized.
source: We first looked at whether the average number of repetitive ensheathments for an axonal domain is different based on whether a sheath becomes stabilized. However, we found that there was no significant difference for this parameter (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The stabilization rate is 20.5% when dividing all stabilized domains by the number of total ensheathment attempts.
source: We then divided all stabilized domains by the number of total ensheathment attempts and this results in an a relatively low stabilization rate of 20.5% (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative calculation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Only one in five ensheathment attempts is stabilized on average by the end of the imaging paradigm at 3 dpf.
source: This means that only one in five ensheathment attempts is stabilized on average by the end of the imaging paradigm at 3 dpf.
evidence: Inference from the 20.5% stabilization rate calculation.

claim: For instances when the process maintained contact with the axon, 65.1% resulted in a stabilized sheath.
source: However, for the instances when the process maintained contact with the axon, 65.1% of these resulted in a stabilized sheath (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Continuous axonal contact might promote sheath stabilization.
source: This suggests that continuous axonal contact might promote sheath stabilization.
evidence: Inference drawn from the higher stabilization rate when processes maintain contact.

claim: Oligodendrocytes extensively explore the axonal environment to find targets that are primed for sheath formation.
source: Collectively, this data supports a model where oligodendrocytes extensively explore the axonal environment to find targets that are primed for sheath formation.
evidence: Interpretation and model based on the repetitive ensheathment data.

claim: No relationship was found between axon diameter and the number of times it was ensheathed (R2 value was 0.01).
source: The R2 value was 0.01 regardless of whether the ensheathment was stabilized or not. Thus, we found no relationship between these parameters in our data (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: Supported by linear regression analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Oligodendrocytes have an initial phase of immature sheath accumulation, followed by a phase of sheath stabilization and loss.
source: As in published studies (Czopka et al., 2013), we found that oligodendrocytes have an initial phase of immature sheath accumulation (Figure 4B), followed by a phase of sheath stabilization and loss (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 4 and consistent with prior literature.

claim: The accumulation phase was very dynamic with a significant number of ensheathments eventually lost.
source: However, the accumulation phase was very dynamic in our studies, with a significant number of ensheathments eventually lost.
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data showing extensive ensheathment loss.

claim: Only 5 out of 19 ensheathment attempts were stabilized for the outlined region of the cell in Figure 4B.
source: For example, only 5 out of 19 ensheathment attempts were stabilized for the outlined region of the cell in Figure 4B (# 10, 13, 14, 18, and 19, Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of the region shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The conditions of the imaging paradigm did not change the final sheath number or average sheath length of oligodendrocytes.
source: Additionally, quality control experiments determined that the conditions of this imaging paradigm did not change the final sheath number or average sheath length of these cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, see Materials and methods for further details).
evidence: Supported by quality control experiment data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The number of hours over which each cell accumulates sheaths ranged from ~4 to 8 hr.
source: However, the number of hours over which each cell accumulates sheaths ranged from ~4 to 8 hr (Figure 5A), making it difficult to combine data from multiple cells for quantitative comparison.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Once an oligodendrocyte accumulated a peak (or maximum) number of immature sheaths, every cell slowed down and stopped forming new sheaths.
source: Thus, once an oligodendrocyte accumulated a peak (or maximum) number of immature sheaths, every cell slowed down and stopped forming new sheaths.
evidence: Observation from time-lapse imaging data.

claim: Dorsal cells accumulated a higher peak number of ensheathments compared to ventral cells.
source: Using this normalization for 19 individual dorsal cells and 18 individual ventral cells, we found that the dorsal cells accumulated a higher peak number of ensheathments compared to the ventral cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by normalized time-lapse data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: ~95% of all ensheathments attempts occurred before reaching peak for both dorsal and ventral groups.
source: Additionally, ~95% of all ensheathments attempts occurred before reaching this peak for both groups (Figure 5C and Figure 5D, vertical dashed line).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: An average of ~100 ensheathment attempts occurred for dorsal cells and ~74 for ventral cells before reaching peak.
source: This was an average of ~100 ensheathment attempts for dorsal cells and ~74 for ventral cells.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of ensheathment attempts.

claim: ~75% of ensheathments were lost before reaching peak for both dorsal and ventral groups.
source: Interestingly, ~75% of these ensheathments were also lost before reaching peak for both groups (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figures 5E and 5F.

claim: Oligodendrocytes initiate a remarkable number of immature ensheathments, with only a small percentage maintained by the end of the accumulation phase.
source: Collectively, this data shows that oligodendrocytes initiate a remarkable number of immature ensheathments, with only a small percentage maintained by the end of the accumulation phase.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the quantitative analysis of ensheathment dynamics.

claim: Dorsal oligodendrocytes exhibited more ensheathment attempts, accumulated a higher peak number of immature ensheathments, and maintained more sheaths at the 4 dpf time point compared to ventral cells.
source: Dorsal oligodendrocytes exhibited more ensheathment attempts, accumulated a higher peak number of immature ensheathments, and maintained more sheaths at the 4 dpf time point compared to ventral cells (Figure 6A–E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figures 6A-E.

claim: Dorsal oligodendrocytes also lost more sheaths during the stabilization phase compared to ventral cells.
source: Dorsal oligodendrocytes also lost more sheaths during the stabilization phase compared to ventral cells (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Both dorsal and ventral populations stabilized a similar percentage of ensheathments throughout the accumulation, stabilization, and combined phases.
source: However, both populations stabilized a similar percentage of ensheathments throughout the accumulation, stabilization, and combined phases of our experimental paradigm (Figure 6G–I).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figures 6G-I.

claim: The levels of sheath initiation for each cell are very heterogeneous (ranging from ~20 to 190), but all oligodendrocytes exhibit a similar overall rate of sheath stabilization (~10–20%).
source: Thus, the levels of sheath initiation for each cell are very heterogeneous (ranging from ~20 to 190), but all oligodendrocytes exhibit a similar overall rate of sheath stabilization (~10–20%).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from quantitative analysis of ensheathment dynamics.

claim: Oligodendrocytes made no new sheaths from 3 to 4 dpf during the sheath stabilization phase.
source: We designed a modified ensheathment dynamics imaging paradigm to test this and found that oligodendrocytes made no new sheaths during this time interval (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, see Materials and methods for further details).
evidence: Supported by modified imaging paradigm data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dorsal cells end up with more sheaths at 4 dpf compared to ventral cells due to increased sheath initiation.
source: Collectively, we conclude that dorsal cells end up with more sheaths at 4 dpf compared to ventral cells due to increased sheath initiation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the comparative analysis of dorsal and ventral cells.

claim: A simple linear regression comparing the total number of ensheathment attempts with the final number of sheaths for each cell established high correlation of these parameters (R2 value of ~0.73 for dorsal cells and ~0.83 for ventral cells).
source: Indeed, a simple linear regression comparing the total number of ensheathment attempts with the final number of sheaths for each cell established high correlation of these parameters (R2 value of ~0.73 for dorsal cells and ~0.83 for ventral cells, Figure 6J).
evidence: Supported by linear regression analysis shown in Figure 6J.

claim: For each stabilized ensheathment, there is a relatively predictable number of ensheathments that are lost.
source: Thus, for each stabilized ensheathment, there is a relatively predictable number of ensheathments that are lost.
evidence: Inference from the high correlation between total ensheathment attempts and final sheath number.

claim: While both sheath initiation and loss vary among oligodendrocytes, they are proportionately regulated across all oligodendrocytes.
source: Altogether, these results strongly suggest that while both sheath initiation and loss vary among oligodendrocytes, they are proportionately regulated across all oligodendrocytes.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the consistent stabilization rate despite variable initiation.

claim: The endocytic recycling pathway is responsible for the reuse or turnover of membrane and membrane proteins in a cell.
source: The endocytic recycling pathway is responsible for the reuse or turnover of membrane and membrane proteins in a cell (depicted in Figure 7A).
evidence: Based on established cell biology knowledge.

claim: Rab5, Rab7, and Rab11 regulate the early endosome, late endosome/lysosome, and recycling endosome, respectively.
source: Rab5, Rab7, and Rab11 regulate the early endosome, late endosome/lysosome, and recycling endosome, respectively (Figure 7A).
evidence: Based on established cell biology knowledge.

claim: All three types of endosomes (Rab5+, Rab7+, Rab11+) were present within immature ensheathments.
source: All three types of endosomes were present within immature ensheathments (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Rab5, Rab7, and Rab11 could all potentially play a role in sheath formation.
source: This data suggests that Rab5, Rab7, and Rab11 could all potentially play a role in sheath formation.
evidence: Inference from the presence of these endosomes in immature sheaths.

claim: Rab proteins are GTPases that are active when bound to GTP and inactive when bound to GDP.
source: Rab proteins are GTPases that are active when bound to GTP and inactive when bound to GDP (Müller and Goody, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The rab5CS36N, rab7AT22N, and rab11AS25N dominant-negative point mutations maintain the Rab protein in a GDP-bound 'off' state.
source: Thus, the rab5CS36N, rab7AT22N, and rab11AS25N dominant-negative point mutations maintain the Rab protein in a GDP-bound 'off' state.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of dominant-negative mutations and citation to prior work (Clark et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2007).

claim: The Rab5DN and Rab11DN mutants both decreased the average sheath number per cell without changing average sheath length.
source: We found that the Rab5DN and Rab11DN mutants both decreased the average sheath number per cell without changing average sheath length (Figure 8A–D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figures 8A-D.

claim: Expression of Rab5DN and Rab11DN mutants apparently had no general negative impact on oligodendrocyte development, but they likely regulate a specific aspect of the ensheathment process.
source: Thus, expression of these mutants apparently had no general negative impact on oligodendrocyte development, but they likely regulate a specific aspect of the ensheathment process.
evidence: Inference from the specific effect on sheath number without affecting sheath length.

claim: The Rab7DN mutant had little impact on sheath number or sheath length.
source: On the other hand, the Rab7DN mutant had little impact on sheath number or sheath length (Figure 8A–D), which suggests that the phenotype we observe for the Rab5DN and Rab11DN mutants is specific to the recycling pathway and is not a generic effect of expressing a dominant-negative Rab mutant.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figures 8A-D.

claim: The phenotype observed for the Rab5DN and Rab11DN mutants is specific to the recycling pathway and is not a generic effect of expressing a dominant-negative Rab mutant.
source: On the other hand, the Rab7DN mutant had little impact on sheath number or sheath length (Figure 8A–D), which suggests that the phenotype we observe for the Rab5DN and Rab11DN mutants is specific to the recycling pathway and is not a generic effect of expressing a dominant-negative Rab mutant.
evidence: Inference from the differential effects of Rab7DN versus Rab5DN and Rab11DN.

claim: The over-expression of the Rab5DN mutant did not change the dynamics of the accumulation phase.
source: Unexpectedly, the over-expression of the Rab5DN mutant did not change the dynamics of the accumulation phase. These cells formed and lost the same number of ensheathments during this phase and accumulated ensheathments to a similar peak number compared to the controls (Figure 9A–C, Figure 9—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figures 9A-C and Figure 9—figure supplement 1A-F.

claim: The Rab5DN mutant specifically impacted the stabilization phase (which starts after cells reach peak sheath accumulation).
source: Instead, the Rab5DN mutant specifically impacted the stabilization phase (which starts after cells reach peak sheath accumulation).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of the stabilization phase.

claim: There was a strong trend that the Rab5DN mutant increased the net number of sheaths that were lost from the peak sheath number out to 4 dpf although it was not statistically significant.
source: We found a strong trend that the mutant increased the net number of sheaths that were lost from the peak sheath number out to 4 dpf although it was not statistically significant (Figure 9C–F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figures 9C-F.

claim: Cells over-expressing the Rab5DN mutant stabilized a lower percentage of sheaths in the stabilization phase specifically.
source: Consistent with this trend, cells over-expressing the Rab5DN mutant stabilized a lower percentage of sheaths in the stabilization phase specifically (Figure 9G–I).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figures 9G-I.

claim: The slope of the Rab5DN mutant regression line was significantly lower than for the control group when comparing total ensheathment attempts to final sheath number.
source: A simple linear regression comparing the total ensheathment attempts to the final sheath number showed that the slope of the mutant regression line was significantly lower than for the control group (Figure 9J).
evidence: Supported by linear regression analysis shown in Figure 9J.

claim: The dominant-negative Rab5 mutant expressed from the myrf driver negatively impacts the longitudinal sheath stabilization rate of oligodendrocytes but has little or no impact on initial sheath accumulation.
source: Collectively, we conclude that the dominant-negative Rab5 mutant expressed from the myrf driver negatively impacts the longitudinal sheath stabilization rate of oligodendrocytes but has little or no impact on initial sheath accumulation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the Rab5DN experimental data.

claim: The extensive loss of ensheathments observed contrasts with previous studies reporting that oligodendrocytes maintain most of the sheaths that are formed.
source: The extensive loss of ensheathments that we observed in our experiments seems to contrast with previous studies reporting that oligodendrocytes maintain most of the sheaths that are formed (Czopka et al., 2013; Mensch et al., 2015).
evidence: Comparison with prior literature (Czopka et al., 2013; Mensch et al., 2015).

claim: Previous studies used imaging intervals of 10–20 min and sheaths had to be at least 5 µm in length and stable for >10 min to be counted.
source: Those studies were the first to demonstrate that oligodendrocytes accumulate sheaths over the course of a few hours. However, imaging intervals of 10–20 min were used, and sheaths had to be at least 5 µm in length and stable for >10 min to be counted.
evidence: Description of methods from prior studies (Czopka et al., 2013; Mensch et al., 2015).

claim: Immature ensheathments as short as 2 µm can wrap around axons, and many of these disappear before growing to 5 µm.
source: Our studies show that immature ensheathments as short as 2 µm can wrap around axons, and many of these disappear before growing to 5 µm.
evidence: Supported by the current study's imaging data.

claim: 5 min was the minimum imaging interval necessary to effectively track the dynamics of initial ensheathments.
source: To effectively track the dynamics of these initial ensheathments, 5 min was the minimum imaging interval necessary based on our criteria.
evidence: Methodological determination from the current study.

claim: While oligodendrocytes accumulate sheaths in a relatively short time, this phase is highly dynamic and involves extensive sheath initiation and loss.
source: Our work builds on these earlier studies (Czopka et al., 2013; Mensch et al., 2015) to show that while oligodendrocytes accumulate sheaths in a relatively short time, this phase is highly dynamic and involves extensive sheath initiation and loss.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the current study's data and comparison with prior work.

claim: Myelin sheath formation can be most simply described as a combination of axon adhesion and membrane biogenesis.
source: Myelin sheath formation can be most simply described as a combination of axon adhesion and membrane biogenesis.
evidence: Based on established understanding of myelin formation.

claim: Extensive 'sampling' of axons plausibly finds regions that are ready to be myelinated.
source: This extensive 'sampling' of axons plausibly finds regions that are ready to be myelinated.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the repetitive ensheathment phenomenon.

claim: Successful sheath formation presumably occurs on axons that are primed with the appropriate adhesion molecules needed to facilitate binding and downstream wrapping.
source: Successful sheath formation presumably occurs on axons that are primed with the appropriate adhesion molecules needed to facilitate binding and downstream wrapping.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the data and prior knowledge.

claim: Previous work shows that the disruption of different adhesion molecules in both neurons and oligodendrocytes can result in reduced myelin sheath number.
source: Previous work supports this idea, showing that the disruption of different adhesion molecules in both neurons and oligodendrocytes can result in reduced myelin sheath number (Hughes and Appel, 2019; Elazar et al., 2019; Djannatian et al., 2019; Bartsch et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Axonal vesicular release could be a part of the priming mechanism for myelination.
source: To further build on this concept, axonal vesicular release could be a part of this priming mechanism.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on prior knowledge.

claim: Synaptic adhesion proteins accumulate underneath and around myelin sheaths in axons to promote stability and sheath growth.
source: This is suggested by the observation that synaptic adhesion proteins accumulate underneath and around myelin sheaths in axons to promote stability and sheath growth (Hines et al., 2015; Mensch et al., 2015; Hughes and Appel, 2019; Almeida et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Recent evidence suggests that myelin stimulates vesicular release as part of a feed-forward mechanism to promote myelination.
source: Recent evidence even suggests that myelin stimulates this vesicular release as part of a feed-forward mechanism to promote myelination (Almeida et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The repetitive ensheathment of the same domain of an axon could be part of a mechanism for priming axons.
source: It is tempting to speculate that the repetitive ensheathment of the same domain of an axon could be part of a mechanism for priming axons.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Activity-dependent axonal vesicular release likely plays a larger role in the subsequent phase of sheath stabilization.
source: However, our activity experiment in Figure 3 did not significantly impact the repetitive ensheathment of axons. Therefore, it seems reasonable to conclude that activity-dependent axonal vesicular release likely plays a larger role in the subsequent phase of sheath stabilization.
evidence: Inference from the activity experiment results.

claim: Rab5 regulates the long-term stabilization of sheaths.
source: Our work supports a model where Rab5+, Rab7+, and Rab11+ endocytic endosomes localize to immature ensheathments and that Rab5 regulates the long-term stabilization of sheaths.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the Rab5DN experimental data.

claim: The endocytic recycling pathway could be regulating the localization of adhesion proteins within myelin to help optimize sheath stability.
source: It seems reasonable that the endocytic recycling pathway could be regulating the localization of adhesion proteins within myelin to help optimize sheath stability.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the data and prior knowledge.

claim: The decrease in sheath stability observed when inhibiting Rab5 is consistent with some of the phenotypes reported from disrupting adhesion proteins in myelin.
source: The decrease in sheath stability that we observe when inhibiting Rab5 is consistent with some of the phenotypes reported from disrupting adhesion proteins in myelin (Hughes and Appel, 2019; Elazar et al., 2019; Djannatian et al., 2019; Bartsch et al., 1997).
evidence: Comparison with prior literature.

claim: Previous work showing that the endocytic recycling pathway is critical for the proper localization of myelin proteins such as PLP in oligodendrocyte cultures supports the idea that the pathway regulates protein localization.
source: Previous work showing that the endocytic recycling pathway is critical for the proper localization of myelin proteins such as PLP in oligodendrocyte cultures also supports this idea (Trajkovic et al., 2006; Winterstein et al., 2008; Baron et al., 2015; Krämer et al., 2001; Feldmann et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The recycling of adhesion molecules or other myelin proteins may be most prevalent during the stabilization phase of sheath formation.
source: Our study suggests that the recycling of adhesion molecules or other myelin proteins may be most prevalent during the stabilization phase of sheath formation.
evidence: Inference from the Rab5DN experimental results.

claim: Expression levels of the Rab5DN mutant may have been insufficient to disrupt the early accumulation phase of sheath formation due to the weak myrf driver.
source: However, since we over-expressed a dominant-negative mutant to inhibit Rab5 activity using myrf, which is a specific but weak driver, it is possible that expression levels of the mutant were insufficient to disrupt the early accumulation phase of sheath formation.
evidence: Speculation about potential limitations of the experimental approach.

claim: The possibility that the recycling of adhesion proteins is also important during the early sheath initiation phase cannot be excluded.
source: We therefore cannot exclude the possibility that the recycling of adhesion proteins is also important during the early sheath initiation phase.
evidence: Acknowledgment of experimental limitations.

claim: There are regional differences in the number of ensheathments formed by each oligodendrocyte.
source: It is very intriguing that there are regional differences in the number of ensheathments formed by each oligodendrocyte.
evidence: Observation from the comparative analysis of dorsal and ventral cells.

claim: Dorsal oligodendrocytes are less abundant but produce more ensheathments per cell than ventral oligodendrocytes.
source: Dorsal oligodendrocytes are less abundant but produce more ensheathments per cell than ventral oligodendrocytes.
evidence: Supported by cell count and ensheathment data.

claim: Cells from both dorsal and ventral regions exhibit a similar ratio of ensheathments formed to ensheathments lost.
